title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve large language model responses for conceptual math question-answering in educational settings, and whether more grounded responses are actually preferred by humans. The authors focus on a key tension in AI tutoring: LLMs can generate helpful conversational explanations, but they may hallucinate or produce answers that are misaligned with curriculum materials. The study asks whether adding retrieved textbook content to prompts can increase groundedness, and how that affects perceived response quality.

The intervention is a RAG-based math QA system built using GPT-3.5-turbo and an OpenStax Prealgebra textbook as the retrieval corpus. Student questions were drawn from Math Nation discussion board posts, and the system generated answers under different prompt guidance conditions: no guidance, low guidance, and high guidance, plus an information-retrieval baseline in one study. The authors evaluated outputs in three studies: automated groundedness metrics across 51 real student queries, a human ranking survey in which educators and education technology designers compared response quality and judged groundedness, and a relevance-annotation study examining whether retrieved document relevance predicted groundedness and preference.

The context is middle-school math question-answering, especially for a WhatsApp-based chatbot tutor called Rori used primarily by low-income learners in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana, and Rwanda. However, the empirical evaluation itself used archived student questions and adult raters rather than live student users. The prompts were written for a hypothetical 13-year-old student in grade 8 or 9 living in Ghana, and the retrieved textbook content came from a prealgebra text covering topics such as functions and geometry.

The main conclusion is that RAG can improve perceived response quality, but only when prompting does not force the model to adhere too rigidly to retrieved text. Human raters preferred the low-guidance RAG responses over both unguided and highly guided responses, while high-guidance responses were judged more grounded in the textbook. This suggests a trade-off between groundedness and human preference: the most textbook-faithful responses were not necessarily the most helpful or preferred. The authors argue that designers of AI math QA systems should balance curriculum alignment with conversational usefulness, and they identify faithfulness in educational QA as an important open design and evaluation problem.

identified_tools.name: Rori
identified_tools.description: A WhatsApp-based chatbot math tutor used by middle-school students, with an ITS-style mastery-learning approach for procedural math lessons.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper partners with Rori developers as an application context for adding LLM-based conceptual math question-answering, but does not empirically evaluate Rori itself.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here for generating math tutoring responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Used via the OpenAI API (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) inside a retrieval-augmented generation math QA system to answer real middle-school algebra and geometry questions under none, low, and high guidance prompt conditions.

findings.finding_summary: In a survey of 9 educators and education technology designers, responses generated with retrieval-augmented prompting were preferred most when using low guidance rather than no guidance or high guidance. Across 144 total preference rankings, low guidance beat high guidance in 63.8% of pairwise comparisons, low guidance beat none in 57.5%, and none beat high guidance in 51.7%, indicating a trade-off between groundedness and human preference rather than a monotonic benefit from more grounding.
findings.measure: Human preference rankings of generated math QA responses

findings.finding_summary: Human raters perceived high-guidance RAG responses as more grounded in the retrieved textbook than low-guidance or no-guidance responses. Groundedness differed significantly across conditions (n=153, one-way ANOVA F(2.0, 99.38)=6.65, p=0.001), with mean groundedness scores of 0.52 for none, 0.59 for low, and 0.90 for high on an ordinal 0-2 scale.
findings.measure: Human-annotated groundedness of responses in retrieved textbook content

findings.finding_summary: Automated groundedness metrics increased as prompt guidance increased, showing prompt engineering can manipulate how strongly generated responses align with retrieved textbook text. The paper reports pooled correlations between automated metrics and human annotations as modest: for groundedness, K-F1++ r=0.52, BLEURT r=0.33, and BERTScore r=0.51; for relevance, K-F1++ r=0.31, BLEURT r=0.30, and BERTScore r=0.42.
findings.measure: Correlation of automated groundedness metrics with human annotations
findings.effect_size: K-F1++ r=0.52; BLEURT r=0.33; BERTScore r=0.51; relevance correlations r=0.31, 0.30, 0.42

findings.finding_summary: Retrieved document relevance was positively associated with perceived groundedness of generated responses, but not with human preference rankings. Across 51 queries, the correlation between retrieved document relevance and perceived groundedness was r=0.56 (p<0.001), while the paper reports no significant relationship between relevance and preference; for example, when low-guidance responses were preferred over high-guidance responses, mean relevance was slightly higher but non-significant (diff=0.19, t=-1.45, p=0.15).
findings.measure: Relationship of retrieval relevance to perceived groundedness and preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical multi-study evaluation, but it relies on survey-based human judgments from educators/designers rather than student learning outcomes, with small samples and no randomized trial of learning impact. The study is useful but preliminary.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear differences in preference and groundedness across prompting conditions, but reports no direct student achievement effects and the practical educational impact remains uncertain. Effects are mostly comparative percentages and correlations rather than demonstrated learning gains.
